title: Le garde du corps  (The Jewelry Bodyguard)

segments.t: Outside Juliette Binoche's hotel room in Cannes, Andrea encounters an unyielding private security guard. Tasked with protecting multi-million euro festival jewels, the guard refuses to let anyone pass without strict clearance. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
J'en déduis que les bijoux Chopard sont arrivés. Bonjour.
Qui êtes-vous, madame?
Andréa Martel, l'agent de Juliette Binoche.
Vous devez attendre ici, madame.
Vous n'êtes pas le garde du corps des bijoux?
Je protège la sécurité de la chambre.
Quoi, alors? Antiterrorisme?
Ici Renard. J'ai une certaine Martel à la chambre 403.
Une certaine Martel? Je suis son agent exclusif!
Je vérifie les autorisations.
Ne mettez pas vos grosses pattes partout.
Pas vous, bien sûr.
D'accord, j'ai compris.
C'est bon, vous pouvez entrer.
Merci beaucoup, Renard.
Bonne journée, madame.
Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
J'en déduis que les bijoux Chopard sont arrivés. Bonjour.
'I deduce that the Chopard jewelry has arrived. Hello.' Putting a tiny stand-in that means 'from it' before 'deduce' gives Andrea's opening remark its brisk flair in French.
Qui êtes-vous, madame?
'Who are you, madam?' Inverted 'are-you' with formal 'you' and 'madam' establishes Renard's stiff, textbook security-guard register.
Andréa Martel, l'agent de Juliette Binoche.
'Andrea Martel, Juliette Binoche's agent.' French has no apostrophe-s possessive, so 'Juliette's agent' must always be built as 'the agent of Juliette.'
Vous devez attendre ici, madame.
'You must wait here, madam.' Polite 'you' plus 'must' states a firm rule without needing any preposition between 'wait' and 'here.'
Vous n'êtes pas le garde du corps des bijoux?
'Aren't you the jewelry bodyguard?' Literally 'guard of the body of the jewels,' French spells out 'bodyguard' as a three-word phrase.
Je protège la sécurité de la chambre.
'I protect the security of the room.' Look out for a hotel false friend: in French, 'chamber' is simply the standard everyday term for a hotel room or bedroom.
Quoi, alors? Antiterrorisme?
'What then? Counter-terrorism?' Pairing 'what' with 'then' makes a punchy two-word comeback—closer to 'what is it then?' in English.
Ici Renard. J'ai une certaine Martel à la chambre 403.
'Renard here. I have a certain Martel at room 403.' Over a radio, French starts with 'here Renard' rather than 'Renard here,' and 'a certain' before a surname sounds delightfully dismissive!
Une certaine Martel? Je suis son agent exclusif!
'A certain Martel? I am her exclusive agent!' Repeating his slight in disbelief, Andrea puts 'exclusive' after 'agent' in French for outraged emphasis.
Je vérifie les autorisations.
'I am checking the authorizations.' Simple present 'I check' covers 'I am checking right now'—French has no separate '-ing' present construction.
Ne mettez pas vos grosses pattes partout.
'Do not put your big paws everywhere.' Calling someone's clumsy hands 'big paws' works as the exact same colorful scolding in French and English!
Pas vous, bien sûr.
'Not you, of course.' Literally 'well sure,' those final two words are the go-to French expression for 'of course.'
D'accord, j'ai compris.
'Okay, I understand.' Where English says 'I understand' in the present, French often reaches for 'I have understood' once a message clicks.
C'est bon, vous pouvez entrer.
'It is all right, you can go in.' Opening with 'it is good' is a super-handy green light you'll hear from guards, waiters, and cashiers alike.
Merci beaucoup, Renard.
'Thank you very much, Renard.' Here is a fun surname detail: Renard's family name is also the ordinary French noun meaning 'fox.'
Bonne journée, madame.

'Have a good day, madam.' Dropping 'have a' in French, Renard wishes her 'good daytime'—focusing on the whole span of the day ahead. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.
J'en déduis que les bijoux Chopard sont arrivés. Bonjour.
Qui êtes-vous, madame?
Andréa Martel, l'agent de Juliette Binoche.
Vous devez attendre ici, madame.
Vous n'êtes pas le garde du corps des bijoux?
Je protège la sécurité de la chambre.
Quoi, alors? Antiterrorisme?
Ici Renard. J'ai une certaine Martel à la chambre 403.
Une certaine Martel? Je suis son agent exclusif!
Je vérifie les autorisations.
Ne mettez pas vos grosses pattes partout.
Pas vous, bien sûr.
D'accord, j'ai compris.
C'est bon, vous pouvez entrer.
Merci beaucoup, Renard.
Bonne journée, madame.
Andrea encounters rigorous security outside Juliette Binoche's suite. After radioing for clearance, the taciturn bodyguard Renard grants Andrea access to her star. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
